Actually, I don't think it is a matter of sharp and unsharp areas per-se concerning the projection of the 3D image. If you take a transmission hologram and light it with a laser from the opposite side it was made the real image will focus in space and each part of the image will be in very clear focus but at different planes from the plate. 

The problem is that the outside of the cloud will want to reflect the inner part of the hologram (the part that should be focused in the center of the cloud) thus not only causing a haze on the outside of the cloud but also inhibiting the light to get to the inner part of the cloud where is needs to be reflected from to be focused. Is that what you meant???

Basically to overcome this problem we need to teach each part of the cloud to not refect the light shown on it unless it is focused....

> **Dinesh:** JohnFP wrote:Actually, I don't think it is a matter of sharp and unsharp areas per-se concerning the projection of the 3D image. If you take a transmission hologram and light it with a laser from the opposite side it was made the real image will focus in space and each part of the image will be in very clear focus but at different planes from the plate.Not necessariy so. This is a common eror. An imaged plane H2 with part of the image in front of the plane is not a real image.There is no light actually there, only a divergent waveform. It's often thought that the part infront of the image plane is a real pseudoscopic image while the back part is a virtual orthoscopic image. This can easily be refuted by image planing a long rod as an H2. As the plate is twisted side to side, the two halves of the rod do not twist in opposite directions - as they would if one half is a pseudo and the other an ortho. Also, the image of the rod cannot be focused, showing it to be a virtual image.

Dinesh, with all due respect let's please compare apples to apples. I said nothing about an H2 or an image planed hologram. If you reread more carefully what I wrote you will find I spoke stricktly of a transmisson hologram. Not image planed, rainbow, white light etc... Just a standard transmission hologram. So I am not so sure I made the "common error". To ellaborate. If you take a transmission hologram and illuminate it with the laser from the other side there is definitely light there. This is proven by the fact of taking a white card held parallel to the plane of the hologram plate and moving it toward and away from the plate. Different parts of the image will become focused at different distances from the plate. We all use this technique when finding where we want the image planed axis in creating an H2.

I understand what you are saying about collapsing wavefront but you missed the point I was making about the part of the image that would be focused in the interrior of the cloud gets partially reflected from the very first edge of the cloud it comes into contact with. This is very evedent every day when driving your car in the fog. The fog reflects the light from you headlight right in front of the car, that is as soon as the light hits the first edge of the fog. Even if this light was focused, this effect would be seen.

This is not a subject that I have seen a lot of information on but I am sure anyone whom has tried this technique experiences this problem as Tom stated. No matter which medium you use, the reflective particles (cloud) cannot differentiate between the light the hits it that is supposed to reflect off of it (focused at that point) or the light that hits it and is supposed to pass through to be reflected and focus at a point behind it.

posts.content_md:
Dinesh wrote:
> Not necessariy so. This is a common eror. An imaged plane H2 with part of the image in front of the plane is not a real image.There is no light actually there, only a divergent waveform. It's often thought that the part infront of the image plane is a real pseudoscopic image while the back part is a virtual orthoscopic image. This can easily be refuted by image planing a long rod as an H2. As the plate is twisted side to side, the two halves of the rod do not twist in opposite directions - as they would if one half is a pseudo and the other an ortho. Also, the image of the rod cannot be focused, showing it to be a virtual image.

This is totally erroneous. There's an orthoscopic virtual image behind the image planed H2 and an orthoscopic real image in front of it. A pseudoscopic real image of a pseudoscopic real image becomes orthoscopic, if you catch my drift.

Philosophically that is what I always believed, chapter and verse. Just to be absolutely sure that was true, I verified it by projecting the real image of an embossed hologram (so I wasn't involved in the generation of the image).

I needed a deep image, something more than a few millimeters deep like a credit card holo. I rustled through the archives until I found the classic "Bird and Rock" by John Kaufman, some kind of a bird skull with a long beak, certainly not the pigeons I am accustomed to in my urban environment, perched on a rock with a lot of holes in it. (I believe I mentioned it in a previous post along the Princess Leia thread.)

I interrogated the holo with a mildly divergent He-Ne beam so as to cover a "burned in" area containing the image in front of the hologram information, aimed along the normal, not its nominal 45 degrees reference angle . This geometry threw the + and - 1st order slits out at the nominal 45 degrees from the normal. (I did this so that the reference beam and its pesky 0 order reflection didn't get in the way of my observations.)

I found the +1, or the *real*, slit with a piece of groundglass, and then chased through it until I encountered a focussable image of the beak. **It ain't a "divergent" wavefront that projects an image onto a groundglass, but a real converging one!** Anyone can repeat this at home, the only caveat is that the image has to be a heck of a lot deeper than a Visa Dove!

An image plane hologram incorporates both virtual and real components. How else could there be an image in front of the plane.? 

Before any equations are posted, please check signs.

Dinesh: **this** is what you said above: "An imaged plane H2 with part of the image in front of the plane is not a real image.There is no light actually there, only a divergent waveform."

What I proved is that there is a convergent real image wavefront of the half of the object in front of the hologram. QED. And the part behind the plate is virtual. And both halves are orthoscopic. 

"If you saw the "opposite" image of an image planed H2 by flipping the plate (assuming it isn't blacked), you'd see a pseudoscopic real image." Yeah I've seen enough of them. If you flip the plate over, yes, what was behind will be in front and what was in front will be behind, swapping their real and virtual identities, but this time they're both pseudoscopic.

"It may be that the confusion lies in the simultaneity. It's true that both a pseudoscopic and an orthoscopic image exist simultaneously inside the diffractive structure, but either image is not pseudoscopic and orthoscopic simultaneoulsy." That's true, but the behind the plate is virtual and the front is real. I think where you are having a problem is in believing that a real image can be orthoscopic.

Sorry that you can't let go that you made a blunder. Fire up a laser and try looking at some deep image plane holograms yourself. Better yet make that holo of a rod you're postulating and see what happens. When you do the holo dance in front of it, moving to the right, the front part moves to the left and the rear part to the right. Swinging the plate will do the same.

No doubt that your "floaters" are all real image. If you care to light one up with a laser, you will undoubtedly see the real image focussed on a screen.

The reason I went with normal incidence in my experiment above is so that the reference beam and its reflection were out of the way. Going back into the basement, illuminating the holo with a 45 degree reference, I observed exactly the same thing described above as far as the focussability of the real image.

Don't invoke Bragg when talking about embossed holos, they only have a surface relief, no layering. There always be an image somewhere. But even a reflection or rainbow on thick material will exhibit the same things as I have stated above, except you could never pull off that non-intended reference angle trick because of the Bragg angle requirement.

posts.topic_title: projecting the real image of an hologram
posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.post_subject: projecting the real image of an hologram
posts.content_md:
What got me involved in this thread was this statement: "An imaged plane H2 with part of the image in front of the plane is not a real image.There is no light actually there, only a divergent waveform." My experiment showed that the part of an image plane image in front of a holographic plate really is real!

Looking at the recording of your hologram #2 of the cat image, when the nose is in front of the plate, the wavefront forming the nose is converging on its way to its real focus, and thereafter divergent by the time it gets to the viewer's eyes. It happens to be converging as it passes the through holographic plate and interferes with the reference. After it converges to its focus, then it diverges.

If a groundglass were put in your set up before the plate holder were loaded at the position of the cat's nose there would be a real image focused there. After removing the groundglass, the plateholder is loaded with a plate, which is then exposed, processed, replaced and illuminated with the analogue of the reference beam, an image of the cat's nose would then be focused on the same piece of groundglass replaced where the image of the cat's nose were focused before. (The problem in seeing this is in the background of the reference beam if things are too close to the plate.) This means that the wavefront issuing from the hologram plate is convergent before divergent, as the holographic wavefront is the optical equivalent of the original one.

In an image planing system where the image straddles the holographic plate, the wavefronts of the image from the H1, mirror, or lens are either converging, or already converged and are now diverging, or are at their focus by the time they meet the holographic plate's plane. Illumination during replay will result in them forming virtual or real images. The stuff behind is virtual. The stuff in front is real. They will all be ortho or pseudo simultaneously, ie an ortho real in front with an ortho virtual behind, which flips into a pseudo real in front and a pseudo virtual behind.

All wavefronts by the time they get to the viewers' eyes will be divergent, but some, the ones apparently in front of the plate, will converge to a real focus that can be projected on to a groundglass before they diverge. This refutes your statement above, which is what needed to be straightened out.

I am not sure how the subject wandered away from the original post. Maybe we should start another thead. The original post was simply projecting a real image onto a volume of dust. Ortho, pseude, H2, diverging, convergin etc... is adding confusion, in my opinion.

Basically, as stated by Tom, if you take a real image and project it into a cloud of dust, water vapor, cotton etc... you will notice that the part of the image that needs to be in focus at 10 inches from the plate will be diffracted as soon as it hits the cloud (let's say the cloud starts at 5 inches from the plate). This not only steals light for that image part but causes the cloud to "glow" as 5, 6, 7 etc... inches from the plate producing a haze, if you will, obstructing the image. 

I assume this is why most carrying out the technology now are using 2D objects.
